True Brightness: Moon vs. the Outer Solar System

Why Neptune is way darker than the photos.

Six real NASA photographs, same instrument, same exposure, no per-object stretching. Surface luminance is scale-invariant, so resizing a disk doesn't change how bright it should look; only distance from the Sun and each body's albedo do. One fixed exposure, radiometrically correct. What a camera or an un-adapted eye registers in a single instant.
Not a measured result. The compression curve here (luminance^0.3) is a rough, illustrative stand-in for perceptual adaptation, not a validated model for this scenario. Specifically: the 0.3 exponent is one commonly-cited approximation among several in the psychophysics literature (published fits range roughly 0.3–0.5 depending on study and conditions); the underlying research is largely from point-source and lab stimuli, not extended dim disks against a black field; and no source is cited here because none was verified for this specific case. Treat this tab as "which direction and roughly how much," not a citable number.

Where these actually sit on a lux scale

Illuminance (lux) is a physical measurement of how much light is landing on a surface, independent of how your eye perceives it. Everyday reference points on the left, each planet's real sunlight level on the right, same logarithmic scale (each gridline is 10× the one below it).

Why "true brightness" looks right. Sunlight falls off as 1/distance². The Moon sits at 1 AU; Neptune sits at 30 AU, so about 900× less sunlight reaches it. Surface luminance ≈ illuminance × albedo ÷ π, then gamma-encoded the same way any screen already encodes light, so nothing here is artificially compressed per-object.
Why normal images disagree. Spacecraft cameras auto-expose per target, Neptune shots use exposures roughly 900× longer (or heavily gained) compared to Moon shots, then each frame gets independently contrast-stretched for clarity. That's correct for seeing detail. It's wrong for comparing brightness.
Why the naked-eye tab differs from both, and its limits. Pupil size barely matters here (it only spans ~16x, versus a 900x range in sunlight across these six bodies); the real mechanism is retinal gain adaptation, which compresses perceived brightness. The specific curve used here is an illustrative approximation, not a validated figure for this exact scenario; see the warning under the toggle when this tab is active for specifics. The qualitative point stands regardless of the exact curve: Neptune's ~140 lux is well inside photopic (full-color) vision, more like an overcast afternoon than twilight. It would look dimmer than the Moon but clearly colored and detailed, not dark.

Photos are the user-supplied planetary disk images, embedded directly in this file. Illuminance modeled from the inverse-square law off a ~128,000 lux solar constant at 1 AU; albedos are standard geometric-albedo values per body. Each true-brightness disk applies a single CSS brightness() filter equal to that body's luminance relative to the Moon's, gamma-encoded -- mathematically the same operation as multiplying raw pixel values, just applied in-browser instead of via image processing. This is a physically-grounded approximation for illustration, not a calibrated radiometric dataset. Real cross-instrument photometry (e.g. the 2018 Irwin et al. reprocessing of Neptune's true color) requires flight calibration data this page doesn't have access to.
